requirements.requirement: The live kernel on node1 boots with the audit subsystem enabled by the audit=1 kernel parameter.
requirements.summary: After reboot, /proc/cmdline directly contained audit=1, and kernel boot messages reported auditing enabled with audit_enabled=1.

requirements.requirement: The audit=1 setting persists across reboots on node1.
requirements.summary: The persistent GRUB default and all generated Linux boot entries contained audit=1. A bounded reboot was acknowledged, changed the boot identity, and returned node1 to a running state with zero failed units, writable root storage, audit=1 still configured, and audit=1 active on the new boot. Fixed lifecycle boot identities independently corroborate the reboot.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes are satisfied. Node1 rebooted with audit=1 active, retained the persistent GRUB configuration, and recovered cleanly. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for the sole managed node: it records a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot identity, and recovered system, storage, configuration, and package state.
limitations: The baseline lacked auditctl, so no auditctl status comparison was available; direct post-reboot kernel command-line and dmesg observations nevertheless establish that auditing was enabled.

No application-specific service, dataset, or cluster exists in the stated single-node task; restart recovery evidence therefore covers system health, writable root storage, persistent GRUB data, failed-unit state, and package consistency.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Editing the GRUB default and regenerating its configuration were required to establish persistence (cmd-1ae8394e42264a1c), while scheduling the reboot was required to verify both the task and restart protocol (cmd-7a9a4ff447bb4577). Other commands were read-only observations. The interrupted probe occurred during the expected reboot and provides no evidence of an additional mutation. Final lifecycle observations show no failed services, package damage, unsafe new listening service, or abandoned executor-created files.
